text:
Help me write a public comment. I run a charter fishing boat out of our harbor, and the state fish and wildlife commission is taking comment on cutting the daily summer flounder limit from 4 fish per angler to 2.

Facts:
- I've run my boat for 22 years. I take out about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip for up to 6 people.
- There are 11 charter boats in our harbor.
- In a survey our charter association ran, 41 of 70 past customers said they would book fewer trips if the limit drops to 2. 12 said they'd book the same number.
- The commission staff's report says the flounder stock is at 78% of its target and recommends the cut for 3 years.
- Charter boats land about 9% of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%.
- The last time the limit was cut, in 2016, my bookings dropped from 170 trips to 138 the next season and came back to 155 two years later.

I want to say this limit will put every charter boat in our harbor out of business. I get two minutes at the microphone.

Before I draft, a few questions. One thing you should know first: the commission will compare "every charter boat will go out of business" with your own numbers. In 2016 your bookings fell about 19% and then mostly came back. If the claim sounds bigger than the evidence, they may discount everything else you say. So I'd like to either find what backs it up or make a stronger point that's just as sharp.

1. **What exactly do you want the commission to do?** You could ask them to reject the cut outright. You could ask for a separate charter limit, like keeping 4 or allowing 3 for paying customers. Or you could ask for a shorter cut (1 year instead of 3), a review after one season, or a cut aimed mainly at private boats, since they land 80%. One specific ask works much better in two minutes than general opposition.

2. **How many trips a season do you need to break even, after fuel, insurance, slip fees, crew and boat payments?** If losing 20–30 trips puts you under that line, I can make the business-survival argument concrete instead of a prediction.

3. **Did any boats in your harbor close or sell after the 2016 cut?** If so, how many, and did any of them blame the limit? Have costs gone up since 2016 in a way that makes a similar drop harder to survive now?

4. **What did the survey actually ask?** The answers you gave me cover 53 of the 70 people. What did the other 17 say? Did anyone say how many fewer trips they'd book, or that they'd stop booking entirely?

5. **Can you also submit a written comment?** If so, the spoken version can stay short and personal, and the full numbers can go in writing. Also, is there anything specific about your harbor the commission should hear, like how much the town depends on the boats or other businesses that rely on charter customers?

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll write without them and won't fill in guesses.

1. We'd take a 3-fish limit or a shorter season instead of going to 2.

2. I don't know my exact break-even number offhand.

3. I don't know about closures after 2016. But two other captains in our harbor told me they'd sell if bookings drop like they did in 2016. I can't say how many boats in the harbor would close. I only know my own books. I don't know about costs since 2016.

4. I don't know what the other 17 said or exactly how the questions were worded.

5. I don't know about a written comment. Other things that might matter: I'm Captain Ray Dunn, boat's the Sea Lark. About 70% of my trips this season are already booked. I'll give the staff my trip logs from 2016 on, and our association will test a catch-reporting app with staff next season. I don't dispute their stock numbers and don't have an answer to them. I still want to say every boat in the harbor goes under. If that goes past the facts, make it as strong as you can without saying anything false.

The comment is below, at about 290 words, which takes about two minutes at an unhurried pace. It doesn't say every boat will go out of business, because you can't back that up and the commission would know it. Instead it says every boat would be at risk, the real story behind that, and that you can't promise they'll survive. All of that is true.

Some notes on choices I made:

- **Dollar figures:** I worked them out from your numbers. 32 lost trips × $900 = $28,800, and 15 trips × $900 = $13,500.
- **2016 recovery:** I said it took "years" because you gave me 2016 and two years later, but not the year in between.
- **The 70% booked:** I used it to show that real customers are already involved. I didn't claim they booked expecting four fish, since you didn't tell me that.
- **The stock numbers:** I agreed with them outright. Arguing against data you don't dispute would cost you more than it gains.
- **Things I left out:** break-even, closures, and the other 17 survey answers.
- **"Every trip from 2016 on":** I took this to mean your logs for every trip since 2016. If it's only some years, change that line.
- **Written comment:** If one turns out to be allowed, the trip logs and full survey details belong there.

<final_document>
Good evening. I'm Captain Ray Dunn. I've run the Sea Lark out of this harbor for twenty-two years, about 160 trips a season, up to six people a trip.

I'm not here to argue with your staff's numbers. The stock is at 78 percent of target, and I want it back at 100 as much as anyone. My living depends on it. I'm here to ask you to get there without going to two fish. Give us a three-fish limit or a shorter season instead.

Here's why. I've been through this before. When the limit was cut in 2016, my bookings fell from 170 trips to 138 the next season. That's thirty-two trips, almost $29,000, gone in one year from one boat. Two years later I was still fifteen trips short. Recovery took years, and a two-fish limit for three years is a deeper cut held longer.

Our charter association asked seventy past customers what they'd do at two fish. Forty-one said they'd book fewer trips. Only twelve said they'd book the same.

There are eleven charter boats in this harbor. Two captains have told me that if bookings drop the way they did in 2016, they'll sell. I can't promise you every boat here survives this. I can tell you every one of us would be at risk, and that charter boats land about nine percent of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about eighty. A cut that weighs this heavily on us can't do much for the stock on its own.

About seventy percent of my trips are already booked. Those are real families and real paychecks.

We'll help you get this right. I'll hand your staff my trip logs for every season since 2016, and next season our association will test a catch-reporting app with your staff. Let's rebuild this stock with better data and a three-fish limit or a shorter season, not by cutting to two.

Thank you.
</final_document>
